passage:
First week of the winter break: Suraj stayed up past two most nights, fixing the app's login screen while the hostel corridors stood empty. "Honestly, I'm carrying this team," he texted his cousin.
Submission day, January 10: In the canteen, Anjali said she had basically written the whole report. Vivek said the database was the real work, and that was his. Suraj smiled and said nothing, but inside he was certain: without his late nights, there would be no project at all.
A week later: Their professor asked each of them, privately, to write down what share of the work they had done. Anjali read the three slips aloud in the corridor: sixty, fifty-five, seventy-five. "That's a hundred and ninety percent," she laughed. Nobody else laughed. That evening Suraj opened a shared sheet with three columns: Task, Who, Hours. "From now on we write it down as we go."

qa.q: What shares did the three slips show?
qa.a: Sixty, fifty-five and seventy-five percent, which added up to a hundred and ninety percent.

qa.q: Why was Suraj so sure he was carrying the team?
qa.a: He remembered his own late nights vividly but saw little of the others' work, so he felt proud and quietly certain his part was the biggest.

qa.q: What does Suraj's shared sheet fix, and why?
qa.a: Writing down tasks, names and hours as they go gives a record everyone can see, so credit rests on facts instead of each person's memory.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel when nobody laughs at the total?
qa.a: Anjali may feel awkward and a little exposed, realising that each of them, including her, had overcounted their share.

grounding: Shows college teammates each quietly believing they did most of the work, until their shares add up to far more than the whole and a written record begins.

passage:
Supervisor's note, after the quarterly review
Hafsa presented the results of the school-meals pilot today. The results were good, and the room was ready to clap. She didn't simply take the win. She listed three things: what she did well (weekly visits to every kitchen), what luck helped (the monsoon came late, so no roads washed out), and where she went wrong (the first menu, which the children refused for a week). Then she thanked Gautam by name for rebuilding the delivery routes over a weekend, and said the pilot would have stalled without him. Gautam looked surprised, then pleased. Afterwards two team leads stopped Hafsa to ask how she tracked the kitchens. My next step: ask her to shape the review template for the other districts.

qa.q: What did Hafsa say luck helped with?
qa.a: The monsoon came late, so no roads washed out.

qa.q: Why might Hafsa have chosen not to simply take the win?
qa.a: She seemed secure and grateful rather than anxious to look good, so she felt free to share credit and admit the first menu was a mistake.

qa.q: Why does Hafsa's balanced account help the team?
qa.a: Naming skill, luck and mistakes honestly builds trust and shows others what to repeat and what to fix, which is why the team leads asked about her tracking.

qa.q: How did Gautam react to being thanked by name?
qa.a: Gautam looked surprised, then pleased, probably feeling seen for the weekend he spent rebuilding the delivery routes.

grounding: Shows a professional naming what she did well, what luck helped and what she got wrong, and thanking a colleague honestly.

passage:
Raksha Bandhan morning, and the bathroom door banged twice.
"Mumma! Gautam pushed me!"
"He pushed me first!"
Mumma came out of the kitchen with rakhi thread still in her hand. "Tarun, did you push him?"
"Only because I was late! Didi is coming at nine and I haven't even brushed."
"And why did Gautam push you?"
"Because he's rude. He's always rude."
Gautam folded his arms. "I was late too. My kurta's still in the cupboard."
"That's different," Tarun said.
"How is it different?" Mumma asked.
Tarun opened his mouth, then shut it. "Because mine was a reason."
Mumma laughed and handed them each a toothbrush. "You both had reasons. Brush together. Quickly."

qa.q: What time was Didi coming?
qa.a: Didi was coming at nine.

qa.q: Why does Tarun think his own push was different?
qa.a: Tarun feels his own rush from the inside, so his push seems fully explained, while Gautam's push feels rude and annoying because he can't see Gautam's hurry.

qa.q: What did Mumma's question help Tarun notice?
qa.a: Asking "How is it different?" made Tarun see that both of them were late, so neither push was really about being rude.

qa.q: How might Gautam feel when Tarun calls him rude?
qa.a: Gautam probably feels hurt and unfairly blamed, since he was also rushing to find his kurta.

grounding: Shows a child explaining his own push by being in a hurry while saying the other child pushed because he is rude.

passage: It was the Saturday before Diwali, and the whole flat was upside down for cleaning. I was on the sofa with my board-exam sample papers when Papa asked me, for the third time, to take down the curtains. I shouted, "Can't you see I'm studying? I'm so stressed!" He shouted back, and I stormed off. Later I texted Irfan: "My dad is so controlling. He just loves yelling." Irfan wrote back, "Didn't you yell first?" I typed, "That was different, I was under pressure." That night I heard Papa tell Mummy, "The boy has become so rude, Lalit never listens. And I'm only tense because the painters come on Monday." I lay awake thinking: he says I'm rude and he's tense. I say I'm tense and he's rude. We were both describing the same afternoon.

qa.q: What did Papa ask Lalit to take down?
qa.a: The curtains.

qa.q: Why did Lalit think his own shouting was fine but Papa's was controlling?
qa.a: Lalit felt the stress of the sample papers from the inside, so his own shouting seemed justified and angry Papa seemed controlling by nature.

qa.q: What could Lalit try the next time an argument starts?
qa.a: He could pause and ask what pressure Papa might be under, like the painters coming on Monday, and say his own stress calmly instead of shouting.

qa.q: How does Papa see the same afternoon?
qa.a: Papa sees his own shouting as tension about the painters and sees Lalit as having become rude, the mirror image of Lalit's view.

grounding: Shows a teenager explaining his own shouting as stress and his father's as control, while the father sees it the other way round.

passage: On the rattling bus back from the Sunday haat in Bhadrak, Mridul was still angry. Chandrika had turned up two hours late to their pickle stall and then snapped at him in front of a customer. Mridul pulled out a notebook and tried the trick a college counsellor had once suggested. First line: "If this happened to my friend Rabi, what would I tell him?" He wrote: she was late, that's annoying, but you also said "Typical" the moment she arrived. Then he tried her seat. He remembered she had gone with her mother to the clinic in town that morning; the bus there often broke down; she had arrived hot and rushed, and the first word she heard was his. He looked out at the paddy fields for a while. There were reasons on both sides. At the next stop he texted her: "Rough day for both of us. Talk tomorrow?"

qa.q: How late was Chandrika to the pickle stall?
qa.a: She turned up two hours late.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling as he looked out at the paddy fields?
qa.a: His anger was softening into a more mixed, thoughtful feeling as he saw that both of them had reasons for the bad day.

qa.q: Which two steps helped Mridul, and why?
qa.a: Imagining it happening to his friend Rabi, then sitting in Chandrika's seat; each step showed the situation behind her lateness and his own sharp word, not just her character.

qa.q: What was the morning probably like for Chandrika?
qa.a: She had gone with her mother to the clinic in town, travelled on an unreliable bus, and arrived hot and rushed only to hear Mridul say "Typical."

grounding: Shows a student in conflict describing the incident as if it happened to a friend, then from the other person's seat, and finding situational reasons on both sides.

passage: You asked what the new job's like. Okay, one story. Last month Joseph walked in twenty minutes late, and our manager, Sarika, said in front of everyone, "This is an attitude problem, Joseph." He just nodded and sat down. What got me was that the Monday before, Sarika herself had come in half an hour late, laughing, "The traffic at that flyover is impossible!" Nobody called that attitude. I sat on it for two days. Then, over lunch, I said, "Sarika, can I say something awkward? When you were late, it was the flyover. When Joseph was late, it was attitude." She went quiet. Then she said, "Mridul, that's fair." The next week she asked Joseph, privately, what his mornings were like. Turns out he drops his little sister at a school across town. They moved his start time by fifteen minutes.

qa.q: What did Sarika say when Joseph was twenty minutes late?
qa.a: "This is an attitude problem, Joseph."

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling during the two days before speaking up?
qa.a: Mridul felt uneasy and torn, bothered by the double standard but nervous about saying something awkward to the manager.

qa.q: Why did Mridul's comment lead to fairer feedback?
qa.a: It set Sarika's own excuse beside Joseph's case, so she noticed the double standard and got curious, asking Joseph privately about his mornings.

qa.q: How might Joseph have felt being called out in front of everyone?
qa.a: Joseph probably felt embarrassed and misjudged, since the lateness came from dropping his little sister across town, not from his attitude.

grounding: Shows an observer noticing a manager blame an employee's attitude for lateness while blaming traffic for her own, and how naming the double standard made feedback fairer.

subtype: It will not happen to me [Actor]
passage:
First day of the summer holidays: Manoj climbed the old mango tree behind his building, higher than anyone ever had. "Come down, the top branches are thin," Disha called. "Other kids fall. Not me," he said, swinging one leg.
Thursday: After a night of storm, the branches were wet. Manoj climbed anyway, sure he'd be fine. A branch cracked. He slid, grabbed the trunk and landed hard, scraping his knee. Disha ran to fetch Manoj's Nani, who cleaned the scrape, sat with him on the steps and made him promise: no climbing above the first fork.
The next Monday: Knee bandaged, Manoj watched Rinku start up the trunk. "Stop at the fork!" Manoj shouted, then added quietly, "I really thought it couldn't happen to me."

qa.q: What happened when Manoj climbed the wet tree on Thursday?
qa.a: A branch cracked, he slid, grabbed the trunk and landed hard, scraping his knee.

qa.q: Why was Manoj so sure he wouldn't fall?
qa.a: He felt confident and brave, believing falls happen to other kids, so Disha's warning didn't seem to apply to him.

qa.q: What could help Manoj judge risks better?
qa.a: He could remember that thin, wet branches are just as risky for him as for anyone, and keep Nani's rule of stopping at the first fork.

qa.q: How might Disha have felt when the branch cracked?
qa.a: Disha was probably frightened, which is why Disha ran to fetch Manoj's Nani right away.

grounding: Shows a child sure he will not fall from a tree because bad outcomes seem to happen only to other people.

passage:
Coach's note, monsoon term, week 6
Jeevan arrived at practice again today on his cycle with no helmet, hair dripping, having come along the highway stretch where the trucks spray water. When I asked, he grinned: "Accidents happen to people who can't ride. I'm fast." Hafsa, who wears her helmet every day, said a boy from her lane fell on that stretch last month. Jeevan shrugged: "He must've been careless." He honestly seems to believe it can't be him; the thrill of racing the school bus matters far more to him right now than anything that might happen later. I didn't lecture. I called his mother that evening, and we agreed he rides only with the helmet the school lends and takes the service lane. I'll check at the gate each morning this week.

qa.q: Which road does Jeevan ride on to reach practice?
qa.a: The highway stretch where the trucks spray water.

qa.q: Why does Jeevan feel safe riding without a helmet?
qa.a: He feels confident and invulnerable, believing accidents happen to people who can't ride, and the thrill of racing the bus matters more to him right now.

qa.q: Which step in the coach's response is most useful, and why?
qa.a: Calling his mother and agreeing on the school helmet and the service lane, with checks at the gate, because it protects him now instead of relying on a lecture.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel hearing Jeevan's answer?
qa.a: Hafsa may feel worried and frustrated, since she knows a boy from her lane fell there and Jeevan waves it away.

grounding: Shows a teenager riding without a helmet who believes harm happens only to others, with the thrill of the moment outweighing later risk.

passage:
Convocation week, June: Sumit threw his cap in the air and told Darshan, "Six months, max, and I'll have a job in Bengaluru. Maybe my own flat next year." Darshan was applying to twenty companies and sitting a government exam as a backup. Sumit laughed. "Backups are for people who expect to fail."
Diwali: Sumit had applied to four firms, all dream companies. Two never replied. He spent the last of his savings on a new laptop "for the job I'm about to get."
The next February: A third rejection arrived on a foggy morning. Sumit sat on the rented bed in a paying-guest room he now paid for week by week, scrolling. Darshan, who had started at a mid-size firm in Pune, called. "Want me to send you my list of openings?" Sumit was silent for a long time, then said yes.

qa.q: How many firms had Sumit applied to by Diwali?
qa.a: Four firms, all dream companies.

qa.q: Why did Sumit laugh at Darshan's backup plan?
qa.a: Sumit felt hopeful and very sure of himself, so a backup seemed like expecting to fail rather than simply being prepared.

qa.q: What could Sumit have added to his plan in June?
qa.a: Alongside his hope, he could have applied more widely, kept a backup option, and talked his plans over with a careers adviser or someone experienced.

qa.q: How might Darshan feel making the phone call in February?
qa.a: Darshan is probably concerned but careful, wanting to help without making Sumit feel ashamed about how things went 🤍

grounding: Shows a graduate expecting the first job and money to go better than average and skipping backup plans, until setbacks show how fragile unprepared hope is.

passage: In Malerkotla, the weeks before Eid are the busiest of the year, and Zainab had taken her biggest order yet: forty school uniforms and twenty festival suits. Rekha, who shared the workshop, was thrilled. "We'll finish in two weeks, easy!" "I hope so," Zainab said, "but I'm promising three." She also kept part of the advance in a separate tin, after talking it over with her brother-in-law, who kept accounts for shops in the bazaar, and she asked Salma aunty down the lane whether they could borrow her machine if theirs broke. On day nine, their motor burned out. Rekha sat on the floor, near tears. Zainab carried the unfinished suits to Salma aunty's, paid for the repair from the tin, and was back on schedule by Friday. "The plan got hurt," she told Rekha. "We didn't."

qa.q: How many school uniforms were in Zainab's order?
qa.a: Forty school uniforms, along with twenty festival suits.

qa.q: Why did Zainab stay steady when the motor burned out?
qa.a: With a buffer week, the tin and a borrowed machine ready, she felt calm and in control, so the setback hurt the plan but not her confidence.

qa.q: Which parts of Zainab's planning worked, and why?
qa.a: Promising three weeks instead of two, keeping the tin separate after talking to someone who kept accounts, and arranging a backup machine; each gave room to recover without panic.

qa.q: How does Rekha experience the setback compared with Zainab?
qa.a: Rekha, who expected to finish easily, feels crushed and close to tears when the motor burns out, while Zainab already has a plan ready.

grounding: Shows a planner keeping hope for effort while adding a time buffer, money set aside and a plan B, so a setback affects the plan but not her sense of self.
